# Brain health and dementia

> *A 52-year-old whose mother has dementia asks the question doctors hear again and again: "Doctor,
> what should I eat so I don't get it too?" The answer is not a superfood or a supplement; it starts
> with the blood vessels.*

::: {.callout-note}
## Learning objectives
- Explain how neurodegeneration and cerebral small-vessel disease add together to cause dementia, and
  why lowering the vascular load lowers the total burden.
- Explain why vascular risk control is the best-supported lever, and interpret the Lancet Commission's
  "up to about 45%" estimate without overselling it.
- Distinguish the MIND diet's cohort association from its null prevention trial, and recommend a
  Mediterranean-style pattern as a low-regret choice.
- Evaluate brain supplements against the trial evidence, including those that can cause harm.
- Identify the non-dietary levers with real weight: physical activity, hearing and vision correction,
  and social and mental engagement.
- Recognise weight loss in advanced dementia as part of the illness, explain why tube feeding does not
  help, and refer for a goals-of-care conversation.
:::

## Brain health at a glance {#sec-overview}

**Dementia** is a clinical syndrome of acquired, progressive loss of memory and thinking severe enough
to affect daily life. It is the condition patients most want a food fix for, and careful counselling
matters because the evidence is encouraging in one place and thin in the others. Four messages
summarise the evidence:

- The biggest dietary lever on the brain is vascular: what protects the heart protects the brain.
  Managing blood pressure, glucose, weight, lipids, smoking and activity is the best-supported, most
  actionable advice. It is the same prevention as for heart disease and diabetes (see the
  [*Cardiovascular Disease & Hypertension*](cardiovascular-disease-hypertension.qmd) and
  [*Type 2 Diabetes*](type-2-diabetes.qmd) chapters).
- A brain-healthy eating pattern is a reasonable, low-regret choice, not a proven cure. The cohort
  studies look impressive, but the one prevention trial built to test a brain diet was negative.
- No brain supplement is proven to prevent dementia, and a few can do harm.
- Late in the disease the problem inverts. Weight loss and difficulty eating are an expected part of
  advanced dementia, not a nutritional gap to fill with a feeding tube.

The task here is to recognise the levers, counsel truthfully and refer; no drug names or doses are
needed.

## The science underneath: two pathways, one brain {#sec-dementia-pathways}

Two kinds of brain damage usually run together in dementia.

The first is **neurodegeneration**: the accumulation of abnormal proteins, with loss of synapses and
neurons and brain atrophy. Two proteins accumulate: **amyloid-β**, in plaques between neurons, and
**tau**, in tangles inside them. Neurodegeneration is the dominant picture in Alzheimer's disease.
Its exact causal chain is still debated, so the amyloid-and-tau account is the leading model, not
settled fact.

The second is vascular: damage to the brain's small blood vessels, called **cerebral small-vessel
disease**. Chronic hypertension damages blood vessels and drives stroke (see the
[*Cardiovascular Disease & Hypertension*](cardiovascular-disease-hypertension.qmd) chapter), and it
damages the brain's own small vessels too. Hypertension stiffens and thickens the small
arterioles, which impairs blood flow and injures the surrounding white matter. The result is the
**lacunar strokes** (small, deep infarcts: areas of brain tissue killed by a blocked small vessel)
and white-matter changes seen on scans.

Diabetes adds to the same vascular injury. The hyperglycaemic, insulin-resistant state (see the
[*Type 2 Diabetes*](type-2-diabetes.qmd) chapter) also damages the brain's small vessels and speeds
brain atrophy [@biessels2014diabetesmri]. There is no separate "diabetic dementia".

![Two kinds of damage usually combine to produce dementia. Neurodegeneration (amyloid plaques and tau tangles) and cerebral small-vessel disease (from hypertension and diabetes) each push the brain toward a clinical threshold; because their injury adds together, reducing the vascular load lowers the total burden and can keep a person below the line for longer.](/figures/mechanisms/dementia-two-pathways.svg){#fig-two-pathways}

The two processes rarely occur alone. In older people, **mixed pathology**, more than one disease
process in the same brain, is the rule: most brains examined at post-mortem show it. The safest
reading is that the two kinds of damage add up: vascular injury lowers the threshold at which
neurodegeneration shows as dementia.

::: {.example}
The Nun Study is the classic demonstration. Among people with the *same* amount of Alzheimer
pathology, those who also had small strokes were far more likely to have had dementia in life.
:::

The additive model has a hopeful corollary. We cannot yet clear plaques and tangles with food, but we
*can* reduce the vascular load, and doing so lowers the total burden whichever model of
neurodegeneration turns out to be right.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: food cannot yet clear amyloid plaques or tau tangles. Why can lowering vascular risk still delay dementia?
In older people, mixed pathology is the rule: neurodegeneration and cerebral small-vessel disease
often occur in the same brain. On the safest reading, the two kinds of damage add up, so vascular
injury lowers the threshold at which neurodegeneration shows as dementia, as in the Nun Study.
Reducing the vascular load lowers the total burden and can keep a person below that threshold for
longer, whichever model of neurodegeneration proves right.
:::

## The prevention levers {#sec-dementia-levers}

### Vascular risk: what protects the heart protects the brain {#sec-dementia-vascular}

The cardiometabolic risk factors for heart disease (hypertension, diabetes, high LDL cholesterol,
obesity, smoking and physical inactivity) are also the modifiable drivers of the vascular contribution
to dementia. Nutrition acts on the brain mostly *through* this vascular route, by improving those risk
factors.

The Lancet Commission estimates that up to about 45% of dementia is associated with a set of
modifiable factors across a lifetime [@livingston2024lancet]. The figure is a
**population-attributable estimate**: a theoretical ceiling that assumes these factors are fully causal
and could be eliminated from the whole population. The estimate is easy to oversell. It does not
promise that one person who controls their risk factors cuts their own risk by 45%, and it is not proof
from a trial.

Each risk factor raises risk only modestly, and reducing vascular damage is one of several ways the
factors are thought to act [@livingston2024lancet]. Because each effect is modest, the large number
comes from adding many common exposures across a life, not from one dominant cause. Two further
points make the estimate usable. The largest single contributors are hearing loss, and education and
social factors, not diet. Midlife is also the window that matters most, so prevention is a long game.

The best trial evidence that treating a vascular risk factor protects the brain comes from SPRINT
MIND. Intensively lowering blood pressure significantly reduced **mild cognitive impairment** (a
decline in memory or thinking that falls short of dementia) and the combined measure of mild
impairment or dementia [@sprintmind2019jama]. It did not, on its own, reduce dementia (the trial was
stopped early for its heart benefit, leaving it underpowered for that harder endpoint). Even with that
caveat, it is the strongest signal we have, and it points at the vessels.

### Can a diet prevent dementia? {#sec-dementia-diet}

The belief that a diet can prevent dementia comes from cohort studies. The **MIND diet** is a blend of
Mediterranean and DASH eating that emphasises leafy greens, berries, nuts, wholegrains, fish and olive
oil. In observational cohorts it was linked to a large reduction in Alzheimer's disease: roughly half
the risk in the highest-adherence group [@morris2015mindad]. The result is impressive, and widely
repeated as fact.

A three-year randomised trial of the MIND diet, built specifically to answer the prevention question,
then found no cognitive benefit over a comparison group also nudged toward better eating
[@barnes2023mindrct]. The cohort signal did not survive the trial.

Three explanations fit the gap (see the [*Evidence vs Hype*](evidence-vs-hype.qmd) chapter):

- People who eat well differ in a hundred other ways, some of which could produce the association.
  That is **confounding**: distortion of an association by a third factor linked to both the
  exposure and the outcome.
- Early, undiagnosed disease can dull appetite and worsen diet (reverse causation).
- Three years may be too short.

Which impressive claims survive a randomised trial is rarely obvious in advance.

<div data-island="trial-check" data-src="/diagrams/trial-check.yml"></div>

For a patient, a Mediterranean-style or MIND-style pattern is safe, affordable and good for the heart.
It is reasonable to recommend as a low-regret choice, though not as a proven shield against dementia.

**Multidomain programmes**, which combine diet, exercise, cognitive activity and vascular monitoring,
have improved cognitive test scores in trials such as FINGER [@ngandu2015finger]. Even the best of them
has not shown a reduction in dementia itself, and the benefit probably runs largely through the
vascular arm.

### Do brain supplements prevent dementia? {#sec-dementia-supplements}

Sooner or later the patient asks about a pill. No supplement is proven to prevent dementia, and
several carry a downside:

| Supplement | Claim / rationale | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| B vitamins | Lower homocysteine (an amino acid in the blood); a small study showed slower brain atrophy on scans [@smith2010vitacog] | Large trials found no benefit to memory or thinking [@clarke2014bvitamin]; an imaging change is not a clinical benefit |
| Fish-oil (omega-3) capsules | Omega-3 for the brain | Trials show no cognitive benefit [@sydenham2012cochraneomega3]; eat fish as food: the capsule is not the food |
| Vitamin E | Antioxidant for prevention | No benefit, and at high doses linked to a small increase in death [@miller2005vitamine]; this one can harm |
| Ginkgo biloba | The classic "brain tonic" | A large trial found it did not reduce dementia at all [@dekosky2008gem]; can increase bleeding and interact with blood thinners |
| Coconut oil or "MCT" (medium-chain triglycerides) | Marketed for Alzheimer's | No credible trial evidence, and coconut oil is about 90% saturated fat, so it works against the vascular lever that actually matters |
| "Medical foods" | Marketed for memory | A regulatory category with a lower bar than a medicine; the label is not evidence that the product works |

A claim deserves scepticism when it rests on a blood or scan marker instead of memory itself, on a
small pilot, or on an after-the-fact subgroup.

A patient with a family history may ask about genetic testing for the *APOE* gene, whose variants are
linked to Alzheimer's risk. The answer is that *APOE* is not tested for or acted on in ordinary
prevention. If the worry persists, that is a reason to refer, not to start a supplement.

### Levers beyond the plate {#sec-dementia-beyond}

The worried-well patient deserves the whole picture, and some of the strongest levers are not
dietary:

- physical activity, a headline recommendation for brain health that works partly through the same
  vessels (see the [*Healthy Ageing*](healthy-ageing.qmd) chapter on exercise in older adults);
- correcting hearing and vision, which matters more than most people expect: uncorrected hearing loss
  is one of the largest single modifiable contributors to dementia risk, so "get your hearing and eyes
  checked" is concrete, high-value advice.

Staying socially and mentally engaged, and treating depression and sleep problems, round out the
picture. Building **cognitive reserve** (the brain's capacity to absorb damage before dementia shows)
and social reserve early also helps; it is part of why rising education levels are lowering dementia
rates across generations.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: why does dementia-prevention advice lead with blood pressure and glucose, not with a brain diet?
The vascular lever has the strongest trial signal: in SPRINT MIND, intensive blood-pressure lowering
reduced mild cognitive impairment, although the trial was underpowered to show fewer cases of dementia
itself. Diabetes injures the same small vessels, so glucose control belongs to the same vascular lever.
The MIND diet's halved risk came from cohorts, which confounding and reverse causation can inflate,
and it did not survive a three-year randomised trial. A Mediterranean-style pattern is still worth
recommending as a low-regret, heart-healthy choice, but not as proven prevention.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: B vitamins slowed brain atrophy on scans in a small study. Why is that not a reason to recommend them?
Brain atrophy on a scan is a marker, not memory itself. When B vitamins were tested in large trials,
they brought no benefit to memory or thinking. A claim that rests on a blood or scan marker, a small
pilot or an after-the-fact subgroup deserves scepticism.
:::

## Eating in advanced dementia: when the problem inverts {#sec-dementia-advanced}

Late in the disease the nutrition problem turns upside down. As dementia advances, weight loss and
difficulty eating are expected, driven by the disease itself: most people with advanced dementia
develop an eating problem, and it marks a late stage of the illness [@mitchell2009cascade]. The
instinct, and the family's plea, is to "do something so she doesn't starve", and the ward reflex is to
consider a feeding tube.

The evidence on that reflex is unusually clear. In advanced dementia, tube feeding does not prolong
survival, prevent aspiration pneumonia, heal or prevent pressure ulcers, or improve comfort, and it can
cause harm, including *more* pressure ulcers [@davies2021cochranetubefeeding;
@teno2012pressureulcers]. Geriatrics societies and the Choosing Wisely campaign converge on the same
position: **careful hand feeding**, offering food for comfort, is preferred [@ags2014feedingtubes].

The generalist's task is to recognise the trajectory, explain gently that the weight loss is part of
the illness and not neglect, and refer for a goals-of-care conversation instead of reaching for a tube.

Two things are separate from the tube question and still appropriate: correcting a genuine vitamin
deficiency, and supporting oral intake with feeding help earlier in the disease. A common ward reflex to
watch is routinely thickening fluids for dysphagia. The evidence for routine thickening is weak, so
recognise the reflex and refer to speech therapy instead of assuming it is needed. The
recognise-and-refer posture, and the malnutrition screening behind it, are set out in the
[*Undernutrition & Malnutrition*](undernutrition-malnutrition.qmd) chapter.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: why is the weight loss of advanced dementia not a gap that a feeding tube can close?
The weight loss and difficulty eating are driven by the disease itself and mark its late stage, so they
are not a simple shortfall of intake. In advanced dementia, tube feeding does not prolong survival,
prevent aspiration pneumonia, heal or prevent pressure ulcers, or improve comfort, and it is linked to
more pressure ulcers. Careful hand feeding for comfort, with a referral for a goals-of-care
conversation, is the evidence-based response.
:::

## The Singapore picture {#sec-singapore}

Singapore is ageing quickly, and dementia is common: about 1 in 11 residents aged 60 and over live with
it, and about half of community dementia is still undiagnosed [@subramaniam2025wisedecade]. That
undiagnosed half is the argument for the generalist's recognise-and-refer role. Risk maps onto the
vascular story locally too: dementia is commoner in Indian than Chinese residents, mirroring the higher
burden of diabetes and vascular disease. "Brain health is vascular health" is therefore a message that
fits national diabetes and hypertension efforts.

Two local realities shape counselling. The first is a large local market in over-the-counter "brain
tonics" (ginkgo, fish oil and traditional tonics). Being sold in a pharmacy does not make a product
proven or approved for dementia.

The second is a set of local socio-cultural signals. In a multi-ethnic Singapore cohort, overall diet
quality tracks with better cognition [@huangx2023singaporemec], and regular curry (curcumin) intake has
been associated with lower rates of new cognitive impairment in older Singaporeans [@lu2025curry]. The
curry finding generates a hypothesis; it is not a prescription. Local prevention programmes are
adapting the multidomain approach to Singaporean food and life.

## What should a patient worried about dementia be told? {#sec-close}

Take the fear seriously, then cover four points:

1. Lead with the blood vessels, because what is good for the heart is good for the brain.
2. Offer a Mediterranean-style pattern as a sensible, low-regret choice, while being clear that it is
   not a proven cure.
3. Steer away from brain supplements, which cost money and can occasionally harm.
4. Add the non-food levers that carry real weight, especially activity and getting hearing and vision
   corrected.

If the same family later returns with a relative who is losing weight in advanced dementia, the kind,
evidence-based answer is comfort, not a tube, with a referral for a proper conversation about goals.

## Practise: "what should I eat so I don't get dementia?" {#sec-case}

A 52-year-old whose mother has dementia asks you what diet will prevent it. Her blood pressure is
raised and her fasting glucose is in the prediabetes range. She has read that the MIND diet halves
Alzheimer's risk, and she wants a supplement recommendation. Counsel her truthfully, without selling
false hope. Your choices branch the case.

## Practise: the feeding-tube request {#sec-case-feeding}

Mrs Koh's mother, 84, has advanced dementia and is eating less and losing weight. The family, upset,
asks the team to insert a feeding tube "so she doesn't starve". Decide what the evidence supports and
how to hold this conversation.
